Active Inference and the Free Energy Principle

Today I want to discuss active inference, which is a framework developed by Karl Friston at University College London. The Free Energy Principle provides a unified theory of brain function based on minimizing variational free energy.

Active Inference unifies perception and action under a single principle. The key insight is that biological agents act to minimize surprise, which can be formalized using variational Bayes. This connects to predictive coding, where the brain constantly generates predictions about sensory input and updates beliefs based on prediction errors.

A central concept is the Markov blanket, which is a statistical boundary separating internal states from external states. This allows us to formalize the boundaries of a system.

The mathematics involves variational free energy, which can be expressed as F = E_q[ln q(x) - ln p(x,y)]. This quantity bounds surprise and drives both perception and action.

Recent work by Thomas Parr and colleagues has extended active inference to discrete time settings, published in their 2017 paper "Active Inference: A Process Theory" in Neural Computation. This work has applications in robotics and computational psychiatry.

Tools like PyMDP (https://github.com/infer-actively/pymdp) make it easier to implement active inference models. The framework continues to evolve with contributions from researchers like Maxwell Ramstead at McGill University.

One open question is how to scale active inference to complex, high-dimensional environments. Current approaches include hierarchical models and deep active inference architectures.
